newsitem.title: INDIA: India to act on oil duties, prices soon - analysts.
newsitem.headline: India to act on oil duties, prices soon - analysts.

text.p: India is likely to cut import tariffs for crude oil and may raise them for refined products in a 1997/98 budget statement next Friday, oil analysts said.
If the differentials between crude and product tariffs are restructured adequately it will be a key step toward liberalising the refining industry.
"It is the key thing to look for," said Shrivatsa Kumar, oil sector analyst at Jardine Fleming Broking India in Bombay, "Otherwise, they can't move forward on deregulation."
Also expected soon is an inescapable decision to hike state-controlled product prices, unchanged since world oil prices surged to six year highs in the second half of 1996.
Analysts were confident Finance Minister P.Chidambaram will rejig oil tariffs in the budget, but a politically charged rise in petroleum prices is likely to be dealt with separately.
For clues on what the government plans for products the diesel price factored into the Railways Ministry budget, announced next Wednesday, should give a good idea.
"They've been asked to factor in a 20 percent increase in diesel," said one oil sector analyst for a Bombay brokerage, who requested anonymity.
The long awaited hike in product prices could come any time in the next week to the next four months, analysts said.
"They will probably wait until the budget is approved, so we are really talking about the end of April, or May," R.K. Pachouri, director of Tata Energy Research Institute said.
Rumours have swirled round Indian stock markets in recent days that a price increase was imminent.

President Shanker Dayal Sharma added to the weight of expectancy by singling out the need to clean up the oil pool account deficit in a speech to parliament on the first day of the three-month budget session last Thursday.

Sharma said the oil pool account deficit was likely to reach 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) by March 31, the end of the 1996/97 fiscal year. The Economic Times newspaper earlier this month, quoting Petroleum Ministry officials, said the deficit was an even scarier 184 billion rupees ($5.1 billion).
The oil pool deficit is effectively the amount the government owes oil companies for selling oil products to Indian consumers way below world prices.
Oil companies shoulder the burden of the deficit while they wait for the state to pay them back. But the increasing strain on their liquidity is forcing companies to borrow.
A few analysts were sceptical about how the government would handle the problems it faced.
They believed tariffs would be tinkered with as a short term palliative for the oil pool deficit, rather than as a conscious move to smooth the path for deregulation in the refining sector.
Chidambaram is likely to cut the crude import tariff from 27 percent, possibly significantly, analysts said.
At the same time tariffs on some products could be raised to create a differential whereby the duty on the refined barrel equates to 10 to 15 percent above the duty on crude.

A differential of less than 10 percent would act as a disincentive to companies to build new refineries needed to cope with India's burgeoning oil demand. It would be cheaper for them to carry on importing products.
Currently the import duty on the main products are as follows; gasoline 32 percent, diesel 32 percent, jet fuel 32 percent, fuel oil 32 percent, liquefied petroleum gas 12 percent, and kerosene zero.
Chidambaram is likely to rig the restructured tariff schedule so its impact on the exchequer is as neutral as possible, a research analyst at a foreign brokerage said.
The oil sector in 1996/97 was budgeted to pay around 168.5 billion rupees into government coffers, of which import tariffs accounted for 94 billion and excise duties 47 billion.
